  native storage pools and volumes, Btrfs subvolumes, lifecycle and isolation.
  Consult before creating or changing an Incus instance, profile, disk,
  storage volume, root binding or provisioning helper.
triggerPhrases:
  - "Incus"
  - "Incus disk"
  - "Incus profile"
  - "Incus storage"
  - "container root disk"
  - "native storage volume"
last_verified: "2026-10-19"
---

# Incus: configuration first, storage-driver ownership

Project-local skill authored from the official Incus documentation below;
not an imported third-party skill or a container-sandbox wrapper. Documentation
review is not proof that any example has been applied to this host. Check the
installed client/server version and applicable API extensions before using
version-dependent options.

## Start with the actual declaration

An Incus instance is configured through instance properties, `config`,
`devices` and ordered `profiles`. The CLI exposes this as YAML; do not invent
a separate authoritative YAML file on disk. Incus owns its configuration.

Read both local and expanded instance configuration. Later profiles override
earlier ones; instance-local configuration overrides profiles. Editing a
shared profile affects every instance that uses it. Do not use expanded
configuration as a blind replacement: it flattens inherited settings.

Read-only infrastructure diagnostics, within the assigned maintenance scope:

```sh
incus version
incus config show <instance>
incus config show <instance> --expanded
incus profile show <profile>
incus storage show <pool>
incus storage volume list <pool>
incus storage volume show <pool> container/<instance>
```

Confirm the selected remote, project, instance type, native UUID and stopped
or running state. A name alone is not an identity or authorization proof.
Use `--force-local` only when explicitly diagnosing this host's local daemon.

## Declare native disks under devices

Example fragment for a NEW container's root on an existing Btrfs pool named
`3tched` (not a migration instruction for an existing container):

```yaml
devices:
  root:
    type: disk
    pool: 3tched
    path: /
```

Incus creates the instance's root storage volume at instance creation. Its
Btrfs driver uses a subvolume for a container filesystem volume. Do not
manually create a per-container `.img`, GPT, `losetup` mapping or filesystem
as an assumed prerequisite for this native root declaration.

Additional managed filesystem volumes are separate objects. Create the
custom volume through the supported control plane first; its device then
names the pool, volume and guest mount path:

```yaml
devices:
  data:
    type: disk
    pool: 3tched
    source: identity-data
    path: /data
```

This references an existing custom filesystem volume named `identity-data`;
it does not create that volume. Custom volumes persist independently of the
instance until explicitly deleted. Do not casually share identity-private
volumes. A device with a host-path `source` and no pool is a host-backed
mount, not an Incus-managed custom volume.

For standalone Incus administration, the native commands are
`incus storage volume create <pool> <volume>` (filesystem by default),
`incus storage volume attach <pool> <volume> <instance> <device> <guest-path>`
and `incus config device add <instance> <device> disk pool=<pool> source=<volume> path=<guest-path>`.
These are reference syntax, NOT permission to bypass this repository's
identity-bound provisioning operations. Do not replay them against an
already provisioned identity without the authorized maintenance contract.

## Do not conflate these layers

| Object | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Btrfs pool backing | Existing block device, loop file or Btrfs subvolume; inspect the pool's `source`. |
| Container filesystem volume | Managed filesystem tree; Btrfs driver represents it as a subvolume. No additional loop per volume is needed. |
| Container `type: disk` device | Mount inside the container, not a VM-style emulated partitioned disk. A host block source is mounted, not automatically passed through as guest block hardware. |
| Custom `block` or `iso` volume | Attachable to VMs, not containers. Do not switch instance type to work around this restriction. |
| Btrfs VM disk | Incus uses a backing file because Btrfs does not natively provide block volumes. This is not the container-volume model. |
| Btrfs seeding/sprouting | Separate block-device filesystem operation; a subvolume is not a writable block member for `btrfs device add`. |

A loop backing an entire existing Incus pool does not imply a loop for each
container. Never detach an existing pool backing to satisfy a statement that
container subvolumes need no loops. Do not create new loop-backed pools or
per-container raw images unless that distinct layout is explicitly requested.

An Incus root declaration alone does NOT implement an external immutable
seed plus writable Btrfs member, a GPT two-partition upgrade replica, or a
read-only overlay. Name any conflict between such requirements and native
filesystem volumes before changing the design. Do not silently replace
seeding with copied roots, snapshots, or an OverlayFS provisioning fallback.
Use the `btrfs` skill for actual seed, membership and send/receive mechanics;
Incus owns its managed-volume lifecycle.

## Preserve ownership, lifecycle and admission

- Begin repository operations in the assigned identity's mounted 3tchedFS.
  Discover declared operations and arguments there. Preserve principal,
  session, grants and Cozo identity-to-storage binding. Missing admission is
  not permission to use the local Incus socket or edit Cozo directly.
- Inspect current native configuration and the provisioning owner before
  changing an existing root. Changing the `pool` key is not a storage migration.
  Preserve native UUID, session/key binding, mount ownership and receipts.
- Keep containers unprivileged, their UID/GID mapping, storage ioctl denials
  and existing device allowlist. Do not grant guest block administration,
  nesting, unrestricted host paths or daemon sockets to make storage work.
- Explicit creation may establish approved storage once. Login, boot, start,
  stop, restart, logout and recovery must not allocate new identity leaves
  or add/remove Btrfs members. Restore/verify existing storage instead.
- Do not mutate Incus-owned storage directories or live overlay lower layers
  behind the daemon. Host storage maintenance must use its supported owner,
  exact device/FSID/mount checks and explicit authorized scope.
- Before any receive, verify the intended mounted destination and its FSID;
  an existing directory is insufficient. Never receive into a fallback path
  on the host root filesystem when the intended mount is missing.
- Distinguish source configuration, accepted operation, native state and
  deployed readiness. Report the operation receipt and authoritative result;
  no claim of success from writing YAML alone. Do not auto-start containers,
  change service managers or run test suites merely to install this skill.

## Official references

Consult the version matching the installed daemon where behavior differs.
These upstream pages were reviewed for this skill on 2026-10-19:

- [Instance configuration](https://linuxcontainers.org/incus/docs/main/explanation/instance_config/)
- [Profiles and inheritance](https://linuxcontainers.org/incus/docs/main/profiles/)
- [Disk devices](https://linuxcontainers.org/incus/docs/main/reference/devices_disk/)
- [Btrfs storage driver](https://linuxcontainers.org/incus/docs/main/reference/storage_btrfs/)
- [Storage volume creation, attachment and content-type restrictions](https://linuxcontainers.org/incus/docs/main/howto/storage_volumes/)

name: memory-safety-patterns
description: Implement memory-safe programming with RAII, ownership, smart pointers, and resource management across Rust, C++, and C. Use when writing safe systems code, managing resources, or preventing memory bugs.

# Memory Safety Patterns

Cross-language patterns for memory-safe programming including RAII, ownership, smart pointers, and resource management.

## When to Use This Skill

- Writing memory-safe systems code
- Managing resources (files, sockets, memory)
- Preventing use-after-free and leaks
- Implementing RAII patterns
- Choosing between languages for safety
- Debugging memory issues

## Core Concepts

### 1. Memory Bug Categories

| Bug Type             | Description                      | Prevention        |
| -------------------- | -------------------------------- | ----------------- |
| **Use-after-free**   | Access freed memory              | Ownership, RAII   |
| **Double-free**      | Free same memory twice           | Smart pointers    |
| **Memory leak**      | Never free memory                | RAII, GC          |
| **Buffer overflow**  | Write past buffer end            | Bounds checking   |
| **Dangling pointer** | Pointer to freed memory          | Lifetime tracking |
| **Data race**        | Concurrent unsynchronized access | Ownership, Sync   |

### 2. Safety Spectrum

```
Manual (C) → Smart Pointers (C++) → Ownership (Rust) → GC (Go, Java)
Less safe                                              More safe
More control                                           Less control
```

## Detailed patterns and worked examples

Detailed pattern documentation lives in `references/details.md`. Read that file when the navigation tier above is insufficient.

## Best Practices

### Do's

- **Prefer RAII** - Tie resource lifetime to scope
- **Use smart pointers** - Avoid raw pointers in C++
- **Understand ownership** - Know who owns what
- **Check bounds** - Use safe access methods
- **Use tools** - AddressSanitizer, Valgrind, Miri

### Don'ts

- **Don't use raw pointers** - Unless interfacing with C
- **Don't return local references** - Dangling pointer
- **Don't ignore compiler warnings** - They catch bugs
- **Don't use `unsafe` carelessly** - In Rust, minimize it
- **Don't assume thread safety** - Be explicit

## Debugging Tools

```bash
# AddressSanitizer (Clang/GCC)
clang++ -fsanitize=address -g source.cpp

# Valgrind
valgrind --leak-check=full ./program

# Rust Miri (undefined behavior detector)
cargo +nightly miri run

# ThreadSanitizer
clang++ -fsanitize=thread -g source.cpp
```

| **Memory leak**      | Never free memory                | RAII, GC          |
| **Buffer overflow**  | Write past buffer end            | Bounds checking   |
| **Dangling pointer** | Pointer to freed memory          | Lifetime tracking |
| **Data race**        | Concurrent unsynchronized access | Ownership, Sync   |

### 2. Safety Spectrum

```
Manual (C) → Smart Pointers (C++) → Ownership (Rust) → GC (Go, Java)
Less safe                                              More safe
More control                                           Less control
```

## Detailed patterns and worked examples

Detailed pattern documentation lives in `references/details.md`. Read that file when the navigation tier above is insufficient.

## Best Practices

### Do's

- **Prefer RAII** - Tie resource lifetime to scope
- **Use smart pointers** - Avoid raw pointers in C++
- **Understand ownership** - Know who owns what
- **Check bounds** - Use safe access methods
- **Use tools** - AddressSanitizer, Valgrind, Miri

### Don'ts

- **Don't use raw pointers** - Unless interfacing with C
- **Don't return local references** - Dangling pointer
- **Don't ignore compiler warnings** - They catch bugs
- **Don't use `unsafe` carelessly** - In Rust, minimize it
- **Don't assume thread safety** - Be explicit

## Debugging Tools

```bash
# AddressSanitizer (Clang/GCC)
clang++ -fsanitize=address -g source.cpp

# Valgrind
valgrind --leak-check=full ./program

# Rust Miri (undefined behavior detector)
cargo +nightly miri run

# ThreadSanitizer
clang++ -fsanitize=thread -g source.cpp
```

# FUSE 内核端故障诊断（三层下钻：系统层 → 类型层 → 代码根因层）
…
## 第三节：诊断流程
…
### L2 → L3: 类型层与代码根因层
…
#### Branch E — 多线程 FUSE Daemon 死锁
…
```
结论: daemon 4 个工作线程全部在 pthread_mutex_lock 等待。
…
根因: FUSE daemon 中锁获取顺序不一致，导致多线程死锁，
      文件系统操作完全挂起。
```

#### Branch F — /dev/fuse 设备权限问题

**触发条件**：容器或非 root 用户启动 FUSE daemon 时出现 Permission denied。

```
L2 诊断：
├── 1. ls -la /dev/fuse（设备节点权限）
├── 2. getfacl /dev/fuse（ACL 权限检查）
├── 3. cat /proc/<daemon_pid>/status | grep Cap（daemon 能力集）
├── 4. grep fuse /etc/group（fuse 用户组）
├── 5. groups <daemon_user>（用户所属组）
├── 6. cat /etc/fuse.conf（FUSE 全局配置）
├── 7. capsh --print | grep fuse（进程能力检查）
├── 8. container environment: cat /proc/1/cgroup（容器内 cgroup 检查）
│
└── L3 根因判定：
    ├── /dev/fuse 权限 0600 root:root → 非 root 用户无法访问
    ├── daemon 用户不在 fuse 组 → 缺少 /dev/fuse 访问权限
    ├── 容器内未挂载 /dev/fuse → 设备节点不存在
    ├── 容器缺少 CAP_SYS_ADMIN 或 CAP_MKNOD → 无法操作 FUSE 设备
    ├── user_allow_other 未在 /etc/fuse.conf 启用 → 无法使用 allow_other
    ├── AppArmor/SELinux 阻止 FUSE 操作 → 安全策略限制
    └── daemon 进程 capabilities 被移除 → container runtime 降权
```

**典型输出**：
```
结论: /dev/fuse 权限 0600 root:root，daemon 以非 root 用户
      运行且不在 fuse 用户组中。
      daemon 启动日志显示 "Permission denied" 打开 /dev/fuse。
根因: /dev/fuse 设备节点仅 root 可读写，FUSE daemon
      以普通用户运行且未加入 fuse 组，无法打开设备。
```

#### Branch G — FUSE 内核模块 Bug

**触发条件**：内核 Panic、Oops、soft lockup 与 FUSE 相关，或已知 FUSE 内核 Bug。

```
L2 诊断：
├── 1. dmesg | grep -iE "fuse|libfuse"（内核 FUSE 消息）
├── 2. dmesg | grep -iE "kernel panic|Oops|BUG|soft lockup"（内核异常）
├── 3. cat /sys/module/fuse/version（FUSE 模块版本）
├── 4. uname -r（内核版本）
├── 5. cat /proc/self/mounts | grep fuse（所有 FUSE 挂载）
├── 6. cat /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/abort（abort 状态）
├── 7. test -f /var/crash/vmcore* 2>/dev/null && ls -lh /var/crash/（crash dump 检查）
├── 8. grep -i fuse /var/log/messages | tail -20（系统日志）
│
└── L3 根因判定：
    ├── 已知 FUSE 内核 Bug 列表匹配（CVE-xxxx-xxxx / 内核 commit）
    ├── 特定内核版本 + FUSE 版本组合已知不兼容
    ├── CR2 地址在 FUSE 模块区域内 → FUSE 内核模块导致 Panic
    ├── soft lockup 栈显示在 fuse_* 函数中 → FUSE 内核路径问题
    ├── 大规模并发操作触发的竞态条件 → 内核 FUSE 并发 Bug
    └── FUSE 模块参数不合理导致内核异常 → max_read 过小/过大
```

**典型输出**：
```
结论: dmesg 显示 "kernel BUG at fs/fuse/dev.c:1234"，
      内核版本 5.15.0-rc3 存在已知 FUSE 并发访问 Bug。
      CR2 地址 0xffff888123456789 在 fuse_dev_do_write 函数范围内。
根因: 内核 FUSE 模块在特定内核版本下存在并发竞态条件，
      多线程并发写操作触发内核 BUG。
```

#### Branch H — 混合/复杂 FUSE 故障

**触发条件**：多种现象共存，或以上分支无法覆盖的复杂 FUSE 问题。

```
L2 诊断：
├── 1. 执行所有以上分支的 L2 诊断（汇总所有证据）
├── 2. 交叉对比各分支症状（判定主次故障）
├── 3. 完整 strace -f -e trace=all -p <daemon_pid> -o /tmp/strace.log
├── 4. lsof -p <daemon_pid>（daemon 打开的文件/连接）
├── 5. tcpdump -i any host <backend_storage_ip>（后端存储网络抓包）
├── 6. strace -e trace=all ls -la <mount_point> 2>&1（客户端操作全追踪）
├── 7. 对比故障前后的 FUSE 配置快照（连接数、参数、daemon 版本）
│
└── L3 根因判定：
    ├── 按故障链优先级排序（先解决依赖的下层问题）
    ├── 多故障串联（daemon 崩溃 → 残留连接 → 新 daemon 无法挂载）
    ├── 配置错误叠加（max_read 过小 + 线程池太小 + writeback 未启用）
    ├── 环境变化触发（内核升级、cgroup 限制、SELinux 策略变更）
    └── 复杂的 libfuse API 使用错误（回调注册、会话管理、信号处理）
```

**典型输出**：
```
结论: 多种故障共存：daemon 线程池过小（4 线程）导致写性能差，
      同时 max_read=4K 进一步退化读性能，writeback cache 启用
      但 daemon 未正确处理 ->write 回调。
根因: 多重配置叠加导致 FUSE 极端性能退化，建议逐一修复：
      1. 增大线程池至 16+
      2. 设置 max_read=128K+
      3. 检查 writeback cache 回调实现
```

---

## 第四节：故障模式速查表

| 故障模式 | 核心命令 | 特征日志/现象 |
|---------|---------|-------------|
| Daemon 崩溃 EIO | `stat <mount_point>` | `Transport endpoint is not connected` |
| 请求队列阻塞 | `cat .../connections/*/waiting` | `waiting > 0` 且持续增长 |
| max_read/write 不当 | `cat .../connections/*/max_read` | `max_read=4096` 性能异常低 |
| writeback 不一致 | `mount \| grep writeback_cache` | 写入后读取数据不同 |
| 多线程死锁 | `cat /proc/<pid>/task/*/stack` | `pthread_mutex_lock` 全部阻塞 |
| /dev/fuse 权限 | `ls -la /dev/fuse` | `Permission denied` |
| 内核 Bug | `dmesg \| grep -i fuse` | `kernel BUG at fs/fuse/dev.c` |
| 混合故障 | 汇总所有诊断 | 多种现象并存 |

## 第五节：参考文档

- `references/fuse_commands.md` — FUSE 诊断命令速查
- `references/fuse_params.md` — 内核 FUSE 相关参数说明
- `references/fuse_patterns.md` — FUSE 故障模式与正则匹配

    ├── 多故障串联（daemon 崩溃 → 残留连接 → 新 daemon 无法挂载）
    ├── 配置错误叠加（max_read 过小 + 线程池太小 + writeback 未启用）
    ├── 环境变化触发（内核升级、cgroup 限制、SELinux 策略变更）
    └── 复杂的 libfuse API 使用错误（回调注册、会话管理、信号处理）
```

**典型输出**：
```
结论: 多种故障共存：daemon 线程池过小（4 线程）导致写性能差，
      同时 max_read=4K 进一步退化读性能，writeback cache 启用
      但 daemon 未正确处理 ->write 回调。
根因: 多重配置叠加导致 FUSE 极端性能退化，建议逐一修复：
      1. 增大线程池至 16+
      2. 设置 max_read=128K+
      3. 检查 writeback cache 回调实现

| 故障模式 | 核心命令 | 特征日志/现象 |
|---------|---------|-------------|
| Daemon 崩溃 EIO | `stat <mount_point>` | `Transport endpoint is not connected` |

| 内核 Bug | `dmesg \| grep -i fuse` | `kernel BUG at fs/fuse/dev.c` |
| 混合故障 | 汇总所有诊断 | 多种现象并存 |

- `references/fuse_params.md` — 内核 FUSE 相关参数说明

# Rust Memory Optimization Guide
…
## Anti-Patterns
…
```rust
// Bad: cloning a large Vec just to avoid lifetime complexity
let data = original.clone(); // expensive and unnecessary

// Good: use Arc or Cow for shared ownership
let data: Arc<[u8]> = original.into();
```

```rust
// Bad: allocating inside a hot loop
for item in items {
    let s = format!("processing {}", item); // allocates every iteration
}

// Good: reuse a buffer
let mut buf = String::with_capacity(128);
for item in items {
    buf.clear();
    write!(buf, "processing {}", item).unwrap();
}
```

- Replacing every `Vec` with `SmallVec` without measuring.
- Keeping arena references after reset.
- Cloning strings to satisfy ownership instead of shortening borrow scopes.
- Using `Arc` as a default clone workaround.
- Optimizing layout for types created a handful of times.
- Using `Box<dyn Trait>` when generics would eliminate the allocation entirely.

## Review Prompt

When reviewing memory optimization, ask what was measured, which allocation is removed, what lifetime assumptions changed, and whether the new type increases stack size or API complexity.

## Optimization Checklist

- Measure allocations before changing data structures.
- Preallocate collections only when capacity is known or bounded.
- Prefer borrowing and `Cow` before cloning strings or buffers.
- Use arenas only when lifetimes are truly batch-scoped.
- Check stack growth when replacing heap allocations with inline storage.
- Re-benchmark after changes and keep the simpler version if gains are noise.
- Profile with `dhat` or `heaptrack` to find actual allocation hotspots.
- Consider `hashbrown` or `rustc-hash` for HashMap-heavy code.

- [Rust Performance Book: Heap Allocations](https://nnethercote.github.io/perf-book/heap-allocations.html)

- [arrayvec](https://docs.rs/arrayvec)

- [compact_str](https://docs.rs/compact_str)
- [bytes](https://docs.rs/bytes)

name: systematic-debugging
description: Use when encountering any bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior, before proposing fixes
---

# Systematic Debugging

## Overview

**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.

**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
```

If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.

## When to Use

Use for ANY technical issue:
- Test failures
- Bugs in production
- Unexpected behavior
- Performance problems
- Build failures
- Integration issues

**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
- You've already tried multiple fixes
- Previous fix didn't work
- You don't fully understand the issue

**Don't skip when:**
- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)

## The Four Phases

You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.

### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation

**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**

1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
   - Don't skip past errors or warnings
   - They often contain the exact solution
   - Read stack traces completely
   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes

2. **Reproduce Consistently**
   - Can you trigger it reliably?
   - What are the exact steps?
   - Does it happen every time?
   - If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess

3. **Check Recent Changes**
   - What changed that could cause this?
   - Git diff, recent commits
   - New dependencies, config changes
   - Environmental differences

4. **Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems**

   **WHEN system has multiple components (CI → build → signing, API → service → database):**

   **BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**
   ```
   For EACH component boundary:
     - Log what data enters component
     - Log what data exits component
     - Verify environment/config propagation
     - Check state at each layer

   Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks
   THEN analyze evidence to identify failing component
   THEN investigate that specific component
   ```

   **Example (multi-layer system):**
   ```bash
   # Layer 1: Workflow
   echo "=== Secrets available in workflow: ==="
   echo "IDENTITY: $([ -n "${IDENTITY:-}" ] && echo SET || echo UNSET)"

   # Layer 2: Build script
   echo "=== Env vars in build script: ==="
   printenv IDENTITY >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "IDENTITY in environment" || echo "IDENTITY not in environment"

   # Layer 3: Signing script
   echo "=== Keychain state: ==="
   security list-keychains
   security find-identity -v

   # Layer 4: Actual signing
   codesign --sign "$IDENTITY" --verbose=4 "$APP"
   ```

   **This reveals:** Which layer fails (secrets → workflow ✓, workflow → build ✗)

5. **Trace Data Flow**

   **WHEN error is deep in call stack:**

   See `root-cause-tracing.md` in this directory for the complete backward tracing technique.

   **Quick version:**
   - Where does bad value originate?
   - What called this with bad value?
   - Keep tracing up until you find the source
   - Fix at source, not at symptom

### Phase 2: Pattern Analysis

**Find the pattern before fixing:**

1. **Find Working Examples**
   - Locate similar working code in same codebase
   - What works that's similar to what's broken?

2. **Compare Against References**
   - If implementing pattern, read reference implementation COMPLETELY
   - Don't skim - read every line
   - Understand the pattern fully before applying

3. **Identify Differences**
   - What's different between working and broken?
   - List every difference, however small
   - Don't assume "that can't matter"

4. **Understand Dependencies**
   - What other components does this need?
   - What settings, config, environment?
   - What assumptions does it make?

### Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing

**Scientific method:**

1. **Form Single Hypothesis**
   - State clearly: "I think X is the root cause because Y"
   - Write it down
   - Be specific, not vague

2. **Test Minimally**
   - Make the SMALLEST possible change to test hypothesis
   - One variable at a time
   - Don't fix multiple things at once

3. **Verify Before Continuing**
   - Did it work? Yes → Phase 4
   - Didn't work? Form NEW hypothesis
   - DON'T add more fixes on top

4. **When You Don't Know**
   - Say "I don't understand X"
   - Don't pretend to know
   - Ask for help
   - Research more

### Phase 4: Implementation

**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**

1. **Create Failing Test Case**
   - Simplest possible reproduction
   - Automated test if possible
   - One-off test script if no framework
   - MUST have before fixing
   - Use the `superpowers:test-driven-development` skill for writing proper failing tests

2. **Implement Single Fix**
   - Address the root cause identified
   - ONE change at a time
   - No "while I'm here" improvements
   - No bundled refactoring

3. **Verify Fix**
   - Test passes now?
   - No other tests broken?
   - Issue actually resolved?
   - Use the `superpowers:verification-before-completion` skill before claiming success

4. **If Fix Doesn't Work**
   - STOP
   - Count: How many fixes have you tried?
   - If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information
   - **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**
   - DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion

5. **If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture**

   **Pattern indicating architectural problem:**
   - Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling/problem in different place
   - Fixes require "massive refactoring" to implement
   - Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere

   **STOP and question fundamentals:**
   - Is this pattern fundamentally sound?
   - Are we "sticking with it through sheer inertia"?
   - Should we refactor architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?

   **Discuss with your human partner before attempting more fixes**

   This is NOT a failed hypothesis - this is a wrong architecture.

## Red Flags - STOP and Follow Process

If you catch yourself thinking:
- "Quick fix for now, investigate later"
- "Just try changing X and see if it works"
- "Add multiple changes, run tests"
- "Skip the test, I'll manually verify"
- "It's probably X, let me fix that"
- "I don't fully understand but this might work"
- "Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently"
- "Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]"
- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow
- **"One more fix attempt" (when already tried 2+)**
- **Each fix reveals new problem in different place**

**ALL of these mean: STOP. Return to Phase 1.**

**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (see Phase 4.5)

## your human partner's Signals You're Doing It Wrong

**Watch for these redirections:**
- "Is that not happening?" - You assumed without verifying
- "Will it show us...?" - You should have added evidence gathering
- "Stop guessing" - You're proposing fixes without understanding
- "Ultra-think this" - Question fundamentals, not just symptoms
- "We're stuck?" (frustrated) - Your approach isn't working

**When you see these:** STOP. Return to Phase 1.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Issue is simple, don't need process" | Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs. |
| "Emergency, no time for process" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |
| "Just try this first, then investigate" | First fix sets the pattern. Do it right from the start. |
| "I'll write test after confirming fix works" | Untested fixes don't stick. Test first proves it. |
| "Multiple fixes at once saves time" | Can't isolate what worked. Causes new bugs. |
| "Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |
| "I see the problem, let me fix it" | Seeing symptoms ≠ understanding root cause. |
| "One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |

## Quick Reference

| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |
|-------|---------------|------------------|
| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |
| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |
| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |

## When Process Reveals "No Root Cause"

If systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:

1. You've completed the process
2. Document what you investigated
3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)
4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation

**But:** 95% of "no root cause" cases are incomplete investigation.

## Supporting Techniques

These techniques are part of systematic debugging and available in this directory:

- **`root-cause-tracing.md`** - Trace bugs backward through call stack to find original trigger
- **`defense-in-depth.md`** - Add validation at multiple layers after finding root cause
- **`condition-based-waiting.md`** - Replace arbitrary timeouts with condition polling

  Rust language patterns and ecosystem covering ownership, borrowing, lifetimes, error handling (Result/Option, thiserror, anyhow), async with Tokio, traits, generics, serde serialization, Cargo workspaces, and testing. Includes axum web framework, ratatui terminal UI, clap CLI parsing, criterion benchmarking, cargo-deny supply chain security, cargo-dist binary distribution, and release-plz changelog automation.

  Use when writing Rust code, designing ownership models, building async services with Tokio/axum, creating terminal UIs with ratatui, setting up CLI applications with clap, configuring CI/CD pipelines for Rust, benchmarking with criterion, auditing dependencies with cargo-deny, or distributing binaries with cargo-dist.

  source: 'https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/'

# Rust

## Overview

Rust is a systems programming language focused on safety, concurrency, and performance. The ownership system guarantees memory safety without garbage collection, and the type system enforces thread safety at compile time.

**When to use:** Systems programming, web services (axum), CLI tools (clap), terminal UIs (ratatui), WebAssembly, performance-critical applications, anything requiring memory safety without runtime overhead.

**When NOT to use:** Rapid prototyping where compile times matter more than safety, simple scripting tasks, projects where the team has no Rust experience and deadlines are tight.

## Quick Reference

| Pattern             | API / Tool                          | Key Points                           |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Ownership transfer  | `let b = a;`                        | `a` is moved, no longer usable       |
| Borrowing           | `&T` / `&mut T`                     | One mutable OR many immutable refs   |
| Lifetime annotation | `fn f<'a>(x: &'a str) -> &'a str`   | Ties output lifetime to input        |
| Error propagation   | `?` operator                        | Converts and propagates errors       |
| Custom errors       | `thiserror::Error` derive           | Structured error types with Display  |
| Ad-hoc errors       | `anyhow::Result<T>`                 | Context chaining for applications    |
| Async runtime       | `#[tokio::main]`                    | Entry point for async programs       |
| Spawn task          | `tokio::spawn(async { })`           | Concurrent async task execution      |
| HTTP router         | `axum::Router::new().route(...)`    | Composable routing with extractors   |
| Extractors          | `Json<T>`, `Path<T>`, `State<T>`    | Type-safe request parsing            |
| Serialization       | `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]` | serde with format-agnostic derives   |
| CLI parsing         | `#[derive(Parser)]`                 | clap derive API for arg parsing      |
| TUI rendering       | `terminal.draw(\|f\| { })`          | Immediate-mode ratatui rendering     |
| Benchmarking        | `criterion::Criterion`              | Statistical benchmarking framework   |

| Mistake                                 | Correct Pattern                               |
| --------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Returning reference to local variable   | Return owned type or use lifetime parameter   |

| Ignoring `must_use` warnings            | Handle or explicitly discard with `let _ =`   |
| Large enum variants                     | Box the large variant to reduce overall size  |
| `async fn` in traits without bounds     | Add `Send` bound or use `async-trait` crate   |
| Missing `#[tokio::test]` on async tests | Use `#[tokio::test]` instead of `#[test]`     |

# Rust

## Overview

Rust is a systems programming language focused on safety, concurrency, and performance. The ownership system guarantees memory safety without garbage collection, and the type system enforces thread safety at compile time.

**When to use:** Systems programming, web services (axum), CLI tools (clap), terminal UIs (ratatui), WebAssembly, performance-critical applications, anything requiring memory safety without runtime overhead.

**When NOT to use:** Rapid prototyping where compile times matter more than safety, simple scripting tasks, projects where the team has no Rust experience and deadlines are tight.

## Quick Reference

| Pattern             | API / Tool                          | Key Points                           |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Ownership transfer  | `let b = a;`                        | `a` is moved, no longer usable       |
| Borrowing           | `&T` / `&mut T`                     | One mutable OR many immutable refs   |
| Lifetime annotation | `fn f<'a>(x: &'a str) -> &'a str`   | Ties output lifetime to input        |
| Error propagation   | `?` operator                        | Converts and propagates errors       |
| Custom errors       | `thiserror::Error` derive           | Structured error types with Display  |
| Ad-hoc errors       | `anyhow::Result<T>`                 | Context chaining for applications    |
| Async runtime       | `#[tokio::main]`                    | Entry point for async programs       |
| Spawn task          | `tokio::spawn(async { })`           | Concurrent async task execution      |
| HTTP router         | `axum::Router::new().route(...)`    | Composable routing with extractors   |
| Extractors          | `Json<T>`, `Path<T>`, `State<T>`    | Type-safe request parsing            |
| Serialization       | `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]` | serde with format-agnostic derives   |
| CLI parsing         | `#[derive(Parser)]`                 | clap derive API for arg parsing      |
| TUI rendering       | `terminal.draw(\|f\| { })`          | Immediate-mode ratatui rendering     |
| Benchmarking        | `criterion::Criterion`              | Statistical benchmarking framework   |
| Dep auditing        | `cargo deny check`                  | License, vulnerability, source audit |
| Binary release      | `cargo dist init`                   | Cross-platform binary distribution   |
| Changelog           | `release-plz update`                | Auto semver bump and changelog       |

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake                                 | Correct Pattern                               |
| --------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |

| Shared mutable state without sync       | Use `Arc<Mutex<T>>` or channels               |
| `String` where `&str` suffices          | Accept `&str` in function parameters          |
| Ignoring `must_use` warnings            | Handle or explicitly discard with `let _ =`   |
| Large enum variants                     | Box the large variant to reduce overall size  |
| `async fn` in traits without bounds     | Add `Send` bound or use `async-trait` crate   |
| Missing `#[tokio::test]` on async tests | Use `#[tokio::test]` instead of `#[test]`     |

content.text:
# Shared physical seed and private leaves

## Manual provisioning checkpoint: partitioned instance disk

The current GPT workflow uses a sparse QEMU raw image under
`/var/lib/incus/storage-pools/3tched-pool`. This must be the top-level Btrfs
mount (`FSROOT /`, root ID 5, inode 256) with filesystem UUID
`a1ab7b42-12a8-437c-8f65-d0469892c8dd`, backed by the Incus pool image
`/var/lib/incus/disks/3tched.img`. The logical Incus pool is still `3tched`.
The host root filesystem is not an acceptable fallback; symlink aliases,
unmounted directories and another filesystem are rejected. A root:root0755
pool root is supported, but `.provisioning` remains root:root0700 and its
receipts and instance images remain root:root0600. V4 adoption also verifies
that the instance image is on the pinned pool filesystem.

The shared seed is the separate protected LVM volume
`/dev/mapper/3tched--vg-3tched--seed`, UUID
`8468cc14-a5e4-409c-96f6-1e157d470ab5`. It must remain SEEDING and block
read-only; no instance identity or Cozo binding is written into it. Adoption
resolves the unique physical partition or LVM volume rather than a UUID alias
that may point at its loop, and verifies the read-only loop's complete backing
against that physical source. Linux 6.17 and newer cannot mount the standalone
seed and a sprouted filesystem simultaneously; the host mount owner must
reconcile the standalone seed mount and its boot declaration before pairing.
This is not permission to modify the seed or replace its read-only loop proof.

The completed image preparation step is available through the provisioner:

```sh
sudo ./deploy/scripts/provision-workspace-subscriber.sh --prepare-disk 3tchedCtlChatbot
sudo ./deploy/scripts/provision-workspace-subscriber.sh --inspect-disk 3tchedCtlChatbot
sudo ./deploy/scripts/provision-workspace-subscriber.sh --prepare-filesystems 3tchedCtlChatbot \
  --seed-device /dev/disk/by-uuid/8468cc14-a5e4-409c-96f6-1e157d470ab5
```

Preparation creates a 60 GiB sparse raw image with GPT: 20 GiB root and the
remaining approximately 40 GiB upgrade partition. `--root-gib` and
`--upgrade-gib` select capacities on a new image. The upgrade remainder is
slightly smaller than its requested capacity because GPT and alignment consume
space. The image and a private preparation receipt live in the loop pool;
the receipt pins the image inode and both partition identities. An interrupted
creation retains its intent and image instead of retrying or cleaning them up.
`inspect` does not register or adopt an existing image.

The filesystem stage attaches a read-only loop view of the sealed seed and adds
the blank root partition once as its writable leaf. It inherits the seven seed
subvolumes; it does not copy the root or create replacement agent subvolumes.
Only the upgrade partition is formatted, with one `@` subvolume. Shared and soul
are read-only in the leaf; memory, rules, skills and user are writable. Private
persistence directories are ordinary directories. Both mounts stay attached for
the next manual step. The receipt records loops, mounts and fresh filesystem
UUIDs. Interrupted intents require investigation, and prepared receipts cannot
repeat device-add or formatting. Never modify the seed after leaves depend on it.

Neither stage performs seed transport, Incus creation, identity registration or
startup. They have no identity/backend preflight dependency.
Those later steps remain subject to the owner's manual
script comparison. The existing identity mode described below expects an
unpartitioned leaf and must not be used with this new partitioned image.

The upgrade lifecycle is host → container only, using Btrfs without Unison:

```sh
sudo ./deploy/scripts/provision-workspace-subscriber.sh --pair-upgrade 3tchedCtlChatbot
sudo ./deploy/scripts/provision-workspace-subscriber.sh --sync-upgrade 3tchedCtlChatbot
```

Pairing sends a read-only snapshot of host upgrade `@` on
`/dev/mapper/3tched--vg-3tched--upgrade`, UUID
`7ac6c955-4028-439c-80b4-c55a647abcb4`, to partition 2 during provisioning,
including when the first upgrade is empty. The host's current top-level mount
is `/run/mount/3tched-ct-upgrade`; `@` is read-only and its parent stays writable
for synchronization snapshots. The helper uses the existing host-upgrade mount
alias under the canonical pool's `.mounts` directory.
Subsequent synchronization sends incrementally from the retained
common baseline, including deletions within the upgrade tree. Received baselines stay read-only;
the published upgrade `@` is a writable clone. Transfer intents and prior
versions are retained for recovery; interrupted publication is not retried
automatically. Snapshot retention cleanup is not implemented by this stage.

The base-owned `identity-roots` service selects completed GPT boot receipts,
verifies the existing native UUID/session/key, and invokes `boot` before a
separate container start. It restores existing loop/mount attachments, synchronizes,
then publishes a read-only OverlayFS OS view at `.mounts/NAME/root-view`.
The upgrade layer takes precedence over the seed-root layer; an empty upgrade
uses the installed seed. Patches removing seed files must include OverlayFS
whiteouts: deleting a file from the upgrade tree alone reveals its seed copy.
The Btrfs layers receive the container UID mapping before mounting OverlayFS,
because this kernel rejects mapping the merged overlay. The view is bound at
the Incus-managed `identity-roots` rootfs, preserving its pool definition.
Six agent subvolumes are separately bound into `/agent`; their existing writable
or read-only policies remain in effect, with private persistence bound separately.
User contents are never sent or received. Synchronization detaches stopped OS
views before rotating a lower layer; it never changes Btrfs membership.
Root binding accepts the exact prepared UID and GID mapping (host 1000000,
namespace 0, range 1000000000) from `volatile.idmap.next` when a stopped,
never-started candidate has no `volatile.idmap.current`. If both exist, they
must agree; no guest start is used to manufacture the current map.

The `--prepare-adoption` stage writes the existing V4 plan for the mounted
identity owner's digest-pinned adoption operation; it does not adopt, start,
create a credential, or broaden a grant. The configured chatbot stays
`3tchedCtlChatbot` (logical ID 0); ordinary allocations begin at `ID-1`.
Final adoption and boot receipt formats are unchanged. Application activation
stages the selected helper closure but does not install or enable the
base-owned `identity-roots` service or bootstrap its pool mount. Source
changes alone do not establish installed boot wiring or a completed adoption.

The seed has the seven sibling subvolumes and guest systemd FUSE service.
`@agent_rules/rules/rules.md` and `@agent_user/user/user.md` are initial
per-instance documents: their content is changed in each private writable leaf,
not in the sealed seed. Shared owner links expose cognitive memory, skills,
routing and plugins without granting authority or starting those features.

## Earlier unpartitioned-leaf integration

The following describes the earlier helper contract. Its device paths,
host-owned FUSE attachment and early backend gates are not the new manual
partitioned-disk workflow and still require reconciliation before automation.

Identity provisioning uses one immutable Btrfs seed on the physical partition
currently named `/dev/sdb2`. Each container has its own writable leaf. A leaf
stores that container's changes; it does not contain a copied root filesystem.
Golden preparation includes the wrapper and its helpers under `libexec/3tched`;
after release activation, the operator entrypoint is
`/usr/local/libexec/3tched/provision-workspace-subscriber`.

The seed's top-level layout is `@`, `@agent_memory`, `@agent_rules`,
`@agent_shared`, `@agent_skills`, `@agent_soul`, and `@agent_user`. Provisioning
uses these existing subvolumes in the sprout. It does not create snapshots,
send/receive root filesystems, copy seed images, or use an overlay root.
Readonly loop views reference the same physical partition bytes.

`provision-workspace-subscriber.sh` first verifies the mounted operator
3tchedFS session and sealed catalog, then calls the declared identity inventory
and provisioning preflight operations through their `call` files. It checks
the operation receipts before invoking the read-only
`op-identity-root seed-preflight`, followed by `seed-profile`, before creating
an empty Incus instance with the `3tched-lungs` profile.
The helper checks the physical seed identity, SEEDING flag and block read-only
state, and refuses a direct mount of the physical source. The wrapper holds
a per-session lock; the helper serializes seed loop setup and leaf creation.
`seed-create` adds the new private writable leaf once. Later starts mount
that existing leaf; stopping does not remove a Btrfs member. Failed starts
also retain membership. The bridge only verifies externally mounted storage;
its `attached` field describes logical attachment, not device membership.
The session hostname and private persistence are
created through the sprout, so those writes belong to the leaf. Persistence is
an ordinary mode-0700 directory at `@agent_user/persist`, bound to the guest's
`/opt/run-mounts/persist`. Provisioning creates no subvolumes at all: only the
seven inherited members are used. Agent soul,
and shared subvolumes remain protected in the guest view. Rules and user
preferences are instance-specific and writable in each private leaf.

Storage receipts identify this layout as `shared-partition-siblings-v2` and
pin its inherited subvolume identities plus the persistence directory's inode,
parent subvolume identity, sprout FSID and image metadata digest. The directory must remain on its
parent filesystem and cannot be a symlink, separate mount, or subvolume.
Older v1 receipts with an extra `@persist` subvolume and snapshot-based receipts are
rejected; this change does not silently migrate them or replace existing
container roots. Existing live persistence and older containers are neither
deleted nor converted; replacement must be prepared separately. Historical
soul reconciliation now verifies existing subvolumes and native devices only,
and fails when they are missing instead of creating them.

Before sealing a new base, `op-identity-image prepare TOP RELEASE_ID
PROVENANCE_JSON` records the archive provenance, offline package inventory,
critical file hashes and exact seven-member layout. It also prepares ordinary
mountpoint directories under `@/run/mount/3tchedFS` and `@/run/opdbus/lungs`.
The helper does not download or verify the archive signature, mount storage,
toggle SEEDING, format devices or create subvolumes. See
[image preparation](../../../deploy/workspace-image/README.md) for its input
contract. Creation fully verifies the pristine image before adding a leaf;
later checks verify the pinned metadata without rejecting legitimate private
package updates in the leaf.

FUSE runs on the host. Fresh provisioning selects a persistent Incus `disk`
device named `3tched`, exposing the session's own host FUSE mount at
`/run/mount/3tchedFS`. The seed needs an empty destination directory, not a
guest FUSE daemon. A native instance UUID pins the host source and process
receipt. An existing legacy hook receipt is verified without silently
converting its attachment mechanism. The common `/etc/3tched` directories
are a separate read-only Incus disk attachment, with links from the inherited
agent subvolumes.

The `3tched-lungs` Incus profile supplies these inherited devices:

```yaml
config: {}
devices:
  runtime-run:
    type: disk
    source: "tmpfs:"
    path: /run
    initial.mode: "0755"
  lungs-socket-dir:
    type: disk
    source: /run/opdbus/lungs
    path: /run/opdbus/lungs
    readonly: "true"
```

The bridge service creates its existing shared socket at
`/run/opdbus/lungs/lungs.sock`. Mounting its dedicated parent directory keeps
socket replacement visible to each guest without exposing other host runtime
files. `seed-profile` creates this exact profile if absent and rejects existing
configuration drift. Provisioning also verifies the inherited devices and
rejects local overrides. The `/run` tmpfs is mounted before its child devices;
image directories alone would not establish that boot ordering.

The bridge creates a root-owned socket with mode 0666 beneath the root-owned
0755 directory. Connection permission allows negotiation; each operation still
requires an authenticated identity and its existing capability grant. Host
`Bind(session)` requires UID 0 in the bridge's own user and PID namespaces.
Guest `BindCurrentContainer()` takes no session argument: it pins the socket's
original process with SO_PEERPIDFD and derives identity from the exact running
native container. Process, native UUID and authoritative identity are checked
again for each call. No SID1 file is installed in the guest.

Clean replacement is scoped to the configured chatbot key and service identity
`b0c777e3-0955-cd8b-3d01-ca12998cae28`, using the provisioner's configured native
alias `3tchedCtlbot`. Hostname remains the session UUID. The old native instance
must be stopped or authoritatively absent, and the new name and leaf must be
unused. Explicit retirement uses `identity_sled.delete_provision_record` through
the operator's mounted namespace, with the existing human write capability
and exact revision. This removes the current row and retains an audit tombstone;
startup respects that tombstone. A version3 plan permits fresh provisioning
from that exact deletion receipt. Ordinary missing rows are not accepted.
After host storage/mount
preparation, the wrapper submits a digest-pinned private plan through the
supported `identity_sled.provision_container` operation. The owner atomically
creates fresh current-schema state and binds it to the new native instance;
legacy persistence and record fields are not imported. Existing external
capability policy remains in force. Normal provisioning starts through
`touch_session`; `--no-start` leaves the fresh identity parked. Only verified
completion receives a boot-ready marker.

If creation fails, `op-identity-root seed-inspect NAME` reports sanitized
receipt metadata and recovery guidance without mounting, formatting or
retrying device-add. Preserve the receipt, base, leaf and mappings until the
recorded intent and actual membership have been reconciled.

Preparing or changing the live seed is a separate operator action. The helper
does not set or clear SEEDING, format the partition, or unmount an unrelated
source mount. Once leaves depend on a seed, that seed must remain unchanged.
At boot, the host storage service uses `seed-readonly` to verify the physical
partition identity and existing SEEDING state, then restore its volatile block
read-only flag before restoring opted-in roots. This never changes filesystem
membership or the SEEDING flag.
The current source change has not been deployed or validated with concurrent
live containers on the fresh base. The September 30 file-backed and physical
seed experiments did demonstrate independent writes, peer-active remounts and
cold loop recreation using distinct read-only views of the same seed on this
…
after deployment; a successful build alone is not a workflow validation.
…
See the [Btrfs seeding documentation](https://btrfs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Seeding-device.html).

receipts and instance images remain root:root0600. V4 adoption also verifies
that the instance image is on the pinned pool filesystem.

The shared seed is the separate protected LVM volume
`/dev/mapper/3tched--vg-3tched--seed`, UUID
`8468cc14-a5e4-409c-96f6-1e157d470ab5`. It must remain SEEDING and block
read-only; no instance identity or Cozo binding is written into it. Adoption
resolves the unique physical partition or LVM volume rather than a UUID alias
that may point at its loop, and verifies the read-only loop's complete backing
against that physical source. Linux 6.17 and newer cannot mount the standalone
seed and a sprouted filesystem simultaneously; the host mount owner must
reconcile the standalone seed mount and its boot declaration before pairing.
This is not permission to modify the seed or replace its read-only loop proof.

The completed image preparation step is available through the provisioner:

```sh
sudo ./deploy/scripts/provision-workspace-subscriber.sh --prepare-disk 3tchedCtlChatbot
sudo ./deploy/scripts/provision-workspace-subscriber.sh --inspect-disk 3tchedCtlChatbot
sudo ./deploy/scripts/provision-workspace-subscriber.sh --prepare-filesystems 3tchedCtlChatbot \
  --seed-device /dev/disk/by-uuid/8468cc14-a5e4-409c-96f6-1e157d470ab5
```

Preparation creates a 60 GiB sparse raw image with GPT: 20 GiB root and the
remaining approximately 40 GiB upgrade partition. `--root-gib` and
`--upgrade-gib` select capacities on a new image. The upgrade remainder is
slightly smaller than its requested capacity because GPT and alignment consume
space. The image and a private preparation receipt live in the loop pool;
the receipt pins the image inode and both partition identities. An interrupted
creation retains its intent and image instead of retrying or cleaning them up.
`inspect` does not register or adopt an existing image.

The filesystem stage attaches a read-only loop view of the sealed seed and adds
the blank root partition once as its writable leaf. It inherits the seven seed
subvolumes; it does not copy the root or create replacement agent subvolumes.
Only the upgrade partition is formatted, with one `@` subvolume. Shared and soul
are read-only in the leaf; memory, rules, skills and user are writable. Private
persistence directories are ordinary directories. Both mounts stay attached for
the next manual step. The receipt records loops, mounts and fresh filesystem
UUIDs. Interrupted intents require investigation, and prepared receipts cannot
repeat device-add or formatting. Never modify the seed after leaves depend on it.

Neither stage performs seed transport, Incus creation, identity registration or
startup. They have no identity/backend preflight dependency.
Those later steps remain subject to the owner's manual
script comparison. The existing identity mode described below expects an
unpartitioned leaf and must not be used with this new partitioned image.

The upgrade lifecycle is host → container only, using Btrfs without Unison:

```sh
sudo ./deploy/scripts/provision-workspace-subscriber.sh --pair-upgrade 3tchedCtlChatbot
sudo ./deploy/scripts/provision-workspace-subscriber.sh --sync-upgrade 3tchedCtlChatbot
```

Pairing sends a read-only snapshot of host upgrade `@` on
`/dev/mapper/3tched--vg-3tched--upgrade`, UUID
`7ac6c955-4028-439c-80b4-c55a647abcb4`, to partition 2 during provisioning,
including when the first upgrade is empty. The host's current top-level mount
is `/run/mount/3tched-ct-upgrade`; `@` is read-only and its parent stays writable
for synchronization snapshots. The helper uses the existing host-upgrade mount
alias under the canonical pool's `.mounts` directory.
Subsequent synchronization sends incrementally from the retained
common baseline, including deletions within the upgrade tree. Received baselines stay read-only;
the published upgrade `@` is a writable clone. Transfer intents and prior
versions are retained for recovery; interrupted publication is not retried
automatically. Snapshot retention cleanup is not implemented by this stage.

The base-owned `identity-roots` service selects completed GPT boot receipts,
verifies the existing native UUID/session/key, and invokes `boot` before a
separate container start. It restores existing loop/mount attachments, synchronizes,
then publishes a read-only OverlayFS OS view at `.mounts/NAME/root-view`.
The upgrade layer takes precedence over the seed-root layer; an empty upgrade
uses the installed seed. Patches removing seed files must include OverlayFS
whiteouts: deleting a file from the upgrade tree alone reveals its seed copy.
The Btrfs layers receive the container UID mapping before mounting OverlayFS,
because this kernel rejects mapping the merged overlay. The view is bound at
the Incus-managed `identity-roots` rootfs, preserving its pool definition.
Six agent subvolumes are separately bound into `/agent`; their existing writable
or read-only policies remain in effect, with private persistence bound separately.
User contents are never sent or received. Synchronization detaches stopped OS
views before rotating a lower layer; it never changes Btrfs membership.
Root binding accepts the exact prepared UID and GID mapping (host 1000000,
namespace 0, range 1000000000) from `volatile.idmap.next` when a stopped,
never-started candidate has no `volatile.idmap.current`. If both exist, they
must agree; no guest start is used to manufacture the current map.

The `--prepare-adoption` stage writes the existing V4 plan for the mounted
identity owner's digest-pinned adoption operation; it does not adopt, start,
create a credential, or broaden a grant. The configured chatbot stays
`3tchedCtlChatbot` (logical ID 0); ordinary allocations begin at `ID-1`.
Final adoption and boot receipt formats are unchanged. Application activation
stages the selected helper closure but does not install or enable the
base-owned `identity-roots` service or bootstrap its pool mount. Source
changes alone do not establish installed boot wiring or a completed adoption.

The seed has the seven sibling subvolumes and guest systemd FUSE service.
`@agent_rules/rules/rules.md` and `@agent_user/user/user.md` are initial
per-instance documents: their content is changed in each private writable leaf,
not in the sealed seed. Shared owner links expose cognitive memory, skills,
routing and plugins without granting authority or starting those features.

## Earlier unpartitioned-leaf integration

The following describes the earlier helper contract. Its device paths,
host-owned FUSE attachment and early backend gates are not the new manual
partitioned-disk workflow and still require reconciliation before automation.

Identity provisioning uses one immutable Btrfs seed on the physical partition
currently named `/dev/sdb2`. Each container has its own writable leaf. A leaf
stores that container's changes; it does not contain a copied root filesystem.
Golden preparation includes the wrapper and its helpers under `libexec/3tched`;
after release activation, the operator entrypoint is
`/usr/local/libexec/3tched/provision-workspace-subscriber`.

The seed's top-level layout is `@`, `@agent_memory`, `@agent_rules`,
`@agent_shared`, `@agent_skills`, `@agent_soul`, and `@agent_user`. Provisioning
uses these existing subvolumes in the sprout. It does not create snapshots,
send/receive root filesystems, copy seed images, or use an overlay root.
Readonly loop views reference the same physical partition bytes.

`provision-workspace-subscriber.sh` first verifies the mounted operator
3tchedFS session and sealed catalog, then calls the declared identity inventory
and provisioning preflight operations through their `call` files. It checks
the operation receipts before invoking the read-only
`op-identity-root seed-preflight`, followed by `seed-profile`, before creating
an empty Incus instance with the `3tched-lungs` profile.
The helper checks the physical seed identity, SEEDING flag and block read-only
state, and refuses a direct mount of the physical source. The wrapper holds
a per-session lock; the helper serializes seed loop setup and leaf creation.
`seed-create` adds the new private writable leaf once. Later starts mount
that existing leaf; stopping does not remove a Btrfs member. Failed starts
also retain membership. The bridge only verifies externally mounted storage;
its `attached` field describes logical attachment, not device membership.
The session hostname and private persistence are
created through the sprout, so those writes belong to the leaf. Persistence is
an ordinary mode-0700 directory at `@agent_user/persist`, bound to the guest's
`/opt/run-mounts/persist`. Provisioning creates no subvolumes at all: only the
seven inherited members are used. Agent soul,
and shared subvolumes remain protected in the guest view. Rules and user
preferences are instance-specific and writable in each private leaf.

Storage receipts identify this layout as `shared-partition-siblings-v2` and
pin its inherited subvolume identities plus the persistence directory's inode,
parent subvolume identity, sprout FSID and image metadata digest. The directory must remain on its
parent filesystem and cannot be a symlink, separate mount, or subvolume.
Older v1 receipts with an extra `@persist` subvolume and snapshot-based receipts are
rejected; this change does not silently migrate them or replace existing
container roots. Existing live persistence and older containers are neither
deleted nor converted; replacement must be prepared separately. Historical
soul reconciliation now verifies existing subvolumes and native devices only,
and fails when they are missing instead of creating them.

Before sealing a new base, `op-identity-image prepare TOP RELEASE_ID
PROVENANCE_JSON` records the archive provenance, offline package inventory,
critical file hashes and exact seven-member layout. It also prepares ordinary
mountpoint directories under `@/run/mount/3tchedFS` and `@/run/opdbus/lungs`.
The helper does not download or verify the archive signature, mount storage,
toggle SEEDING, format devices or create subvolumes. See
[image preparation](../../../deploy/workspace-image/README.md) for its input
contract. Creation fully verifies the pristine image before adding a leaf;
later checks verify the pinned metadata without rejecting legitimate private
package updates in the leaf.

FUSE runs on the host. Fresh provisioning selects a persistent Incus `disk`
device named `3tched`, exposing the session's own host FUSE mount at
`/run/mount/3tchedFS`. The seed needs an empty destination directory, not a
guest FUSE daemon. A native instance UUID pins the host source and process
receipt. An existing legacy hook receipt is verified without silently
converting its attachment mechanism. The common `/etc/3tched` directories
are a separate read-only Incus disk attachment, with links from the inherited
agent subvolumes.

The `3tched-lungs` Incus profile supplies these inherited devices:

```yaml
config: {}
devices:
  runtime-run:
    type: disk
    source: "tmpfs:"
    path: /run
    initial.mode: "0755"
  lungs-socket-dir:
    type: disk
    source: /run/opdbus/lungs
    path: /run/opdbus/lungs
    readonly: "true"
```

The bridge service creates its existing shared socket at
`/run/opdbus/lungs/lungs.sock`. Mounting its dedicated parent directory keeps
socket replacement visible to each guest without exposing other host runtime
files. `seed-profile` creates this exact profile if absent and rejects existing
configuration drift. Provisioning also verifies the inherited devices and
rejects local overrides. The `/run` tmpfs is mounted before its child devices;
image directories alone would not establish that boot ordering.

The bridge creates a root-owned socket with mode 0666 beneath the root-owned
0755 directory. Connection permission allows negotiation; each operation still
requires an authenticated identity and its existing capability grant. Host
`Bind(session)` requires UID 0 in the bridge's own user and PID namespaces.
Guest `BindCurrentContainer()` takes no session argument: it pins the socket's
original process with SO_PEERPIDFD and derives identity from the exact running
native container. Process, native UUID and authoritative identity are checked
again for each call. No SID1 file is installed in the guest.

Clean replacement is scoped to the configured chatbot key and service identity
`b0c777e3-0955-cd8b-3d01-ca12998cae28`, using the provisioner's configured native
alias `3tchedCtlbot`. Hostname remains the session UUID. The old native instance
must be stopped or authoritatively absent, and the new name and leaf must be
unused. Explicit retirement uses `identity_sled.delete_provision_record` through
the operator's mounted namespace, with the existing human write capability
and exact revision. This removes the current row and retains an audit tombstone;
startup respects that tombstone. A version3 plan permits fresh provisioning
from that exact deletion receipt. Ordinary missing rows are not accepted.
After host storage/mount
preparation, the wrapper submits a digest-pinned private plan through the
supported `identity_sled.provision_container` operation. The owner atomically
creates fresh current-schema state and binds it to the new native instance;
legacy persistence and record fields are not imported. Existing external
capability policy remains in force. Normal provisioning starts through
`touch_session`; `--no-start` leaves the fresh identity parked. Only verified
completion receives a boot-ready marker.

If creation fails, `op-identity-root seed-inspect NAME` reports sanitized
receipt metadata and recovery guidance without mounting, formatting or
retrying device-add. Preserve the receipt, base, leaf and mappings until the
recorded intent and actual membership have been reconciled.

Preparing or changing the live seed is a separate operator action. The helper
does not set or clear SEEDING, format the partition, or unmount an unrelated
source mount. Once leaves depend on a seed, that seed must remain unchanged.
At boot, the host storage service uses `seed-readonly` to verify the physical
partition identity and existing SEEDING state, then restore its volatile block
read-only flag before restoring opted-in roots. This never changes filesystem
membership or the SEEDING flag.
The current source change has not been deployed or validated with concurrent
live containers on the fresh base. The September 30 file-backed and physical
seed experiments did demonstrate independent writes, peer-active remounts and
cold loop recreation using distinct read-only views of the same seed on this
…
after deployment; a successful build alone is not a workflow validation.
…
See the [Btrfs seeding documentation](https://btrfs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Seeding-device.html).
